page.title: tinyactors: control flow you can test
page.description: Write your program's lifecycles as statecharts, simulate them on a fake clock, check invariants on every run, and run them as millions of actors.

hero.headline: Control flow you can test.
hero.lede: Write your program's lifecycles as statecharts: orders, connections, retries, even your test users. A statechart is formal, so you can simulate it on a fake clock, check invariants after every run, and search for the run that breaks them. tinyactors runs statecharts as actors, from a handful to millions, inside Node.js, Bun, Python, the browser or C.

section.heading: Control flow hides in flags and timers.
section.p: Much of a program is a lifecycle. An order is open, then paying, then paid or timed out. A connection is dialing, up, or backing off. Written as flags, callbacks and timers, a lifecycle spreads over a codebase, and the states it can be in are written down nowhere.

A statechart writes them down: the states, the events that move between them, and what happens on the way. This payment asks a service to charge a card, retries twice when no answer comes within 30 seconds, and then gives up.

section.heading: A thousand runs, no waiting.
section.p: The chart talks to the world only through events, so a test can play the world. A SimulatedClock moves only when the test moves it, so a 30-second timeout costs nothing, and a seeded generator decides when the payment service answers and when it stays silent. This program runs a thousand seeds and checks two invariants in each.

example.caption: Change attempts < 3 to attempts < 4 and seed 10 fails: charged 4 times. The seed reproduces the run that found it.

claim.statement: The semantics are a W3C standard.
claim.p: Charts are written in SCXML, and the core passes all 191 automatic tests of the W3C's SCXML test suite. What a chart does is defined, not whatever the runtime happens to do.

claim.statement: Logic in charts, I/O in your handlers.
claim.p: The host does no I/O of its own. Everything an actor sends out goes to a handler you give it, which does the I/O and answers with an event. The same chart runs against the network in production and against a simulation in a test.

claim.statement: Every transition is a fact you can assert on.
claim.p: Each step an actor takes is a trace span: the event it took, the transitions that fired, the states it entered. granary's integration tests assert on nothing else.

claim.statement: One actor per thing, even for millions of things.
claim.p: With a store and a bound on resident actors, idle actors are hibernated and woken by their next event. A benchmark runs two million actors with a thousand in memory and checks every actor's count after 200,000 events.

section.heading: Statecharts all the way down.
section.p: A lifecycle is not only in your product. The services it calls, the users who use it and the faults that hit it have lifecycles too, and they can be charts as well. granary, a GitHub app that closes issues opened by people not on an allowlist, is built this way.

item.text: One actor per issue: idle → checking → allowed | closing → closed | failed, with its 10-second timeout in the chart.
Its fake GitHub is an actor system, with an actor holding the faults a test injects.
Its load generator's people are charts with a seed: a persistent contributor who reopens and stews, a bot that floods, a chaos monkey, a fuzzer.
Its watchdog is a control loop: ok → suspect → healing → ok.

section.heading: The same charts, in production.
section.p: A host runs your actors on your program's event loop and gives the operator what a long-lived system needs.

item.text: Actors past a resident bound go to your store and come back on their next event.
Add a new version of a chart, and running actors move to it while events keep coming.
The whole host as one blob, restored with its clock, its timers and its actors.
Traces, logs and metrics as OpenTelemetry, with a trace that follows an event across actors and systems.
@tinyactors/node: Node.js 22.3 or later and Bun, on macOS and Linux. Charts in JavaScript, or in the QuickJS sandbox for charts you do not trust.
tinyactors: CPython 3.13 or later. Charts in Python, synchronous or under asyncio.
@tinyactors/wasm: the same API as WebAssembly, for browsers and for platforms with no native addon.
The core embeds anywhere: no C library, no I/O, no threads, and memory only from an allocator you give it.
